claim: The founding lines of the RIAILs were the laboratory strain N2 (Bristol) and the Hawaiian natural isolate CB4856, whose genomes differ at approximately one in ~240 base pairs.
source: The founding lines of the RIAILs were the laboratory strain N2 (Bristol) and the Hawaiian natural isolate CB4856, whose genomes differ at approximately one in ~240 base pairs (Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2019

claim: The panel of 182 RIAILs was generated from ten rounds of random intercrossing, followed by ten rounds of selfing.
source: The panel of 182 RIAILs was generated from ten rounds of random intercrossing, followed by ten rounds of selfing (Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The final RIAIL lines were genotyped at 1,454 markers along the genome.
source: the final lines were genotyped at 1,454 markers along the genome.
evidence: Stated as a methodological fact about the RIAIL panel

claim: Approximately 50 embryos per line were imaged in each of the 182 lines.
source: We imaged ~50 embryos per line in each of the 182 lines (~five replicates per line, ~10 embryos per replicate, Figure 1A)
evidence: Stated as a description of the experimental design

claim: A total of approximately 12,000,000 microscopy pictures were obtained from 3D movies of 9,641 embryos.
source: This resulted in a total of ~12,000,000 microscopy pictures from the 3D movies of the 9,641 embryos that were imaged (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated as a description of the dataset size

claim: The founding C. elegans strains N2 and CB4856 had similar spindle characteristics.
source: The founding C. elegans strains used to create the RIAILs, N2 and CB4856, had similar spindle characteristics (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A; Farhadifar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and citation to Farhadifar et al., 2015

claim: Extensive quantitative variations in spindle characteristics were observed across the RIAIL panel.
source: In contrast, we observed extensive quantitative variations in spindle characteristics across the RIAIL panel (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-E).
evidence: Supported by reference to multiple figures showing variation

claim: Statistically significant broad-sense heritability was found for all spindle traits.
source: We found statistically significant broad-sense heritability (the fraction of variance due to differences between lines) for all spindle traits (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B; Lynch and Walsh, 1998).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and citation to Lynch and Walsh, 1998

claim: The phenotypic similarity of spindle traits in the founding lines N2 and CB4856 results from them having a different genetic basis in those two lines.
source: Thus, there are genetic variations for the spindle and other cell biological traits across the RIAIL panel, and the phenotypic similarity of these traits in the founding lines results from them having a different genetic basis in those two lines.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of genetic variation across RIAILs despite phenotypic similarity in founders

claim: There is a negligible correlation between initial and final spindle length across the RIAILs.
source: To test this prediction, we plotted the average final spindle length vs the average initial spindle length for each of the RIAILs and instead observed a negligible correlation between these two (Figure 2B, p = 0.17).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p = 0.17) and reference to Figure 2B

claim: A Timer model does not explain final spindle length in C. elegans.
source: Thus, a Timer model does not explain final spindle length in C. elegans.
evidence: Concluded from the lack of correlation between initial and final spindle length

claim: The absence of correlation between initial and final spindle length argues against models in which the position of centrosomes in metaphase determine the distribution of forces that control the final length of the spindle.
source: The absence of a correlation between initial and final spindle length also argues against models in which the position of centrosomes in metaphase determine the distribution of forces that control the final length of the spindle (Hara and Kimura, 2009).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation and cited reference to Hara and Kimura, 2009

claim: Final spindle length is highly correlated with cell area across the RIAIL panel.
source: To test this possibility, we plotted final spindle length as a function of the area of the cell measured from DIC images, which is a proxy for cell volume because of the rotational symmetry of the embryo, across the RIAIL panel, and observed a highly significant correlation (Figure 2D, p = 2.97E-36).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p = 2.97E-36) and reference to Figure 2D

claim: Cell area is highly correlated with cell length across the RIAILs.
source: However, cell area is highly correlated with cell length across the RIAILs (Figure 2E, p = 8.38E-73)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p = 8.38E-73) and reference to Figure 2E

claim: There is a negligible partial correlation between final spindle length and cell area conditioned on cell length across the RIAILs.
source: Doing this, we observed a negligible partial correlation between the final spindle length and cell area conditioned on cell length across the RIAILs (Figure 2F, p = 0.13).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p = 0.13) and reference to Figure 2F

claim: Cell volume does not determine final spindle length.
source: Therefore, cell volume does not determine final spindle length, which is inconsistent with the simplest version of the Limiting Component model considered here.
evidence: Concluded from the lack of partial correlation between cell area and final spindle length when conditioned on cell length

claim: Cell length is a critical factor in the regulation of final spindle length in C. elegans.
source: Our analysis so far indicates that cell length is a critical factor in the regulation of final spindle length in C. elegans.
evidence: Concluded from the analysis of correlations and partial correlations

claim: Final spindle length is highly correlated with cell length across the RIAIL panel.
source: To test these predictions, we plot the final spindle length as a function of cell length across the RIAIL panel and find that they are highly correlated as predicted (Figure 2H, p = 7.96E-55).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p = 7.96E-55) and reference to Figure 2H

claim: Final spindle length is positively correlated with centrosome distance.
source: However, final spindle length was also positively correlated with centrosome distance (Figure 2I, p = 6.81E-14)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p = 6.81E-14) and reference to Figure 2I

claim: Centrosome distance is positively correlated with cell length.
source: This inconsistency results from centrosome distance being positively correlated with cell length (Figure 2J, p = 5.25E-31)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p = 5.25E-31) and reference to Figure 2J

claim: The simplest Boundary model does not explain the regulation of final spindle length in C. elegans.
source: Thus, the simplest Boundary model does not explain the regulation of final spindle length in C. elegans.
evidence: Concluded from the positive correlation between final spindle length and centrosome distance, which contradicts the model's prediction

claim: QTL mapping revealed one QTL on chromosome III (QTL1) that influences final spindle length independently of cell length.
source: This conditional QTL mapping revealed one QTL on chromosome III, which we refer to as QTL1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by QTL mapping analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: An additional QTL on chromosome III (QTL2) influences final spindle length independent of both cell length and QTL1.
source: Similar to above, we conditioned final length on both cell length and QTL1, which revealed an additional QTL on chromosome III that we refer to as QTL2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by conditional QTL mapping analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: QTL1 explains 21% of the variation in final spindle length that is independent of cell length.
source: QTL1 explains 21% of the variation across the RIAILs (i.e. heritability) in final spindle length that is independent of the cell length, while QTL2 explains an additional 10%.
evidence: Stated as a result of QTL analysis

claim: QTL2 explains an additional 10% of the variation in final spindle length independent of cell length and QTL1.
source: QTL1 explains 21% of the variation across the RIAILs (i.e. heritability) in final spindle length that is independent of the cell length, while QTL2 explains an additional 10%.
evidence: Stated as a result of QTL analysis

claim: Lines with the N2 allele of QTL1 have shorter final spindles.
source: Lines with the N2 allele of QTL1 have shorter final spindles (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Lines with the N2 allele of QTL2 have longer final spindles.
source: while lines with the N2 allele of QTL2 have longer final spindles (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The N2 alleles of QTL1 and QTL2 have opposite effects on final spindle length.
source: Thus, the N2 alleles of QTL1 and QTL2 have opposite effects on final spindle length (as do the CB4856 alleles).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that N2 allele of QTL1 shortens spindles while N2 allele of QTL2 lengthens them

claim: Final spindle length is the same in N2 and CB4856 despite their different genetic basis for this trait.
source: This is consistent with the observation that final spindle length is the same in N2 and CB4856 despite their different genetic basis for this trait as revealed by the variation across the RIAILs.
evidence: Inferred from the opposite effects of QTL1 and QTL2 alleles and the phenotypic similarity of founders

claim: QTL1 overlapped with the location of gpr-1, which contains two missense variants that differ between N2 and CB4856.
source: QTL1 overlapped with the location of gpr-1, which contains two missense variants (nonsynonymous) that differ between N2 and CB4856 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: GPR-1 regulates pulling forces on astral MTs that drive spindle oscillations, positioning, and elongation.
source: GPR-1 regulates pulling forces on astral MTs that drive spindle oscillations, positioning, and elongation (Hara and Kimura, 2009; Pecreaux et al., 2006; Colombo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hara and Kimura, 2009; Pecreaux et al., 2006; Colombo et al., 2003

claim: gpr-1/2 (RNAi) embryos have shorter final spindle length (17.4±0.2 μm).
source: Consistent with previous results (Hara and Kimura, 2009), we observed that gpr-1/2 (RNAi) embryos have shorter final spindle length (FL = 17.4±0.2 [μm], p = 3.82E-30, Figure 3E, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and statistical analysis (p = 3.82E-30)

claim: QTL2 overlapped with the location of par-2, which contains three missense and two synonymous variants between N2 and CB4856.
source: QTL2 overlapped with the location of par-2, one of the central components of the PAR system in C. elegans (Cuenca et al., 2003), which contains three missense (nonsynonymous) and two synonymous variants between N2 and CB4856 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Cuenca et al., 2003

claim: Lines with the N2 allele of QTL2 have significantly higher PAR-2 transcript abundance than lines with the CB4856 allele.
source: We analyzed previously obtained data from the same panel of RIAILs (Rockman et al., 2010) and found that lines with the N2 allele of QTL2 have significantly higher PAR-2 transcript abundance than lines with the CB4856 allele (p = 6.08E-17, Figure 3—figure supplement 3
evidence: Supported by analysis of transcript data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and statistical analysis (p = 6.08E-17)

claim: par-2 (RNAi) embryos have shorter final spindle length (19.8±0.2 μm).
source: par-2 (RNAi) embryos have shorter final spindle length (FL = 19.8±0.2 [μm], p = 1.03E-22, Figure 3F, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and statistical analysis (p = 1.03E-22)

claim: The PAR system controls the spatial distribution of GPR-1 in C. elegans embryos.
source: Previous studies have shown that the PAR system controls the spatial distribution of GPR-1 in C. elegans embryos (Colombo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colombo et al., 2003

claim: PAR-2 regulates final spindle length.
source: While prior work has described the role of PAR-2 in regulating spindle positioning (Grill et al., 2001), this RNAi knockdown shows that PAR-2 also regulates final spindle length.
evidence: Inferred from the RNAi knockdown experiment showing shorter spindles in par-2 (RNAi) embryos

claim: Cell length is a primary determinant of final spindle length.
source: Taken together, our analysis of the RIAILs shows that cell length is a primary determinant of final spindle length
evidence: Concluded from the analysis of correlations and QTL mapping

claim: Two QTLs influence final spindle length independent of cell length.
source: Taken together, our analysis of the RIAILs shows that cell length is a primary determinant of final spindle length, and identified two QTLs that influence final spindle length independent of cell length.
evidence: Concluded from QTL mapping analysis

claim: The causative genetic variants underlying QTL1 and QTL2 might be in gpr-1 and par-2.
source: Our RNAi knockdown experiments suggest that the causative genetic variants that underly these QTLs might be in gpr-1 and par-2.
evidence: Speculated based on QTL overlap with gene locations and RNAi phenotypes

claim: The spindle elongates until it reaches a length at which pulling forces and other forces acting on centrosomes are in balance.
source: This argues that the spindle elongates until it reaches a length at which pulling forces, and other forces that may be acting on centrosomes, are in balance.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic analysis and known roles of GPR-1 and PAR-2

claim: After cup-cut laser ablation leaving only MTs extending to the cell periphery parallel to the spindle axis, the centrosome moved closer to the cell periphery at an average speed of 14.5±2.8 μm/min.
source: We performed this pattern of ablation on 13 embryos (Figure 4C) and found that the average speed of centrosome motion after the cut was 14.5±2.8 μm/min
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 13 embryos shown in Figure 4C

claim: After cup-cut laser ablation, centrosomes moved an average of 3.9±0.2 μm toward the cell periphery.
source: and that the centrosomes moved an average of 3.9±0.2 μm toward the cell periphery.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from laser ablation experiments

claim: The rapid motion of the centrosome in the direction of the remaining MTs after the cup-cut indicates that there is not a balance of pushing and pulling forces acting on these MTs, rather, they are subject to net pulling forces.
source: The rapid motion of the centrosome in the direction of the remaining MTs after the cup-cut indicates that there is not a balance of pushing and pulling forces acting on these MTs, rather, they are subject to net pulling forces (Figure 4D).
evidence: Inferred from the observed centrosome motion after laser ablation

claim: After plane-cut through the spindle, the average speed of centrosome motion was 1.6±1.0 μm/min.
source: We performed this pattern of ablation on 15 embryos (Figure 4G) and found that the average speed of centrosome motion after the cut was 1.6±1.0 μm/min
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 15 embryos shown in Figure 4G

claim: After plane-cut through the spindle, centrosomes moved an average of 0.7±0.1 μm toward the cell periphery.
source: and that the centrosomes moved an average of 0.7±0.1 μm toward the cell periphery.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from laser ablation experiments

claim: Forces from the spindle have a relatively minor impact on the final position of the centrosomes in C. elegans.
source: This result argues that forces from the spindle have a relatively minor impact on the final position of the centrosomes in C. elegans (Figure 4H).
evidence: Inferred from the small centrosome displacement after spindle ablation

claim: spd-1 (RNAi) embryos lack a central spindle in anaphase.
source: To further test this conclusion, we studied spd-1 (RNAi) embryos, which lack a central spindle in anaphase (Figure 4I, inset) (Verbrugghe and White, 2004)
evidence: Supported by observation shown in Figure 4I inset and citation to Verbrugghe and White, 2004

claim: spd-1 (RNAi) embryos have nearly identical final spindle length to controls (24.5±0.1 μm for spd-1 (RNAi) vs 23.8±0.2 μm for control).
source: and found that their final spindle length is nearly identical to controls (24.5±0.1 μm for spd-1 (RNAi) vs 23.8±0.2 μm for control, p = 2.2E-3) (Figure 4I, Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I and statistical analysis (p = 2.2E-3)

claim: The central spindle has only a very minor impact on final spindle length.
source: Thus, the central spindle has only a very minor impact on final spindle length.
evidence: Concluded from the spd-1 (RNAi) experiment showing nearly identical final spindle length

claim: The final position of the centrosomes is not set by forces from spindle MTs balancing pulling forces from astral MTs.
source: This further argues that the final position of the centrosomes is not set by forces from spindle MTs balancing pulling forces from astral MTs (Figure 4H).
evidence: Inferred from the laser ablation and spd-1 (RNAi) experiments

claim: After perpendicular cup-cut leaving only MTs between the centrosome and the cell periphery perpendicular to the spindle axis, the average speed of centrosome motion was 22.3±4.3 μm/min.
source: We performed this pattern of ablation on 15 embryos (Figure 4L) and found that the average speed of centrosome motion after the cut was 22.3±4.3 μm/min
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 15 embryos shown in Figure 4L

claim: After perpendicular cup-cut, centrosomes moved an average of 6.6±0.3 μm toward the cell periphery.
source: and that the centrosomes moved an average of 6.6±0.3 μm toward the cell periphery.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from laser ablation experiments

claim: Even when centrosome motion has ceased and the spindle has obtained its final length at the end of anaphase, there are pulling forces present both parallel and perpendicular to the spindle axis.
source: Thus, even when centrosome motion has ceased, and the spindle has obtained its final length at the end of anaphase, there are pulling forces present both parallel (Figure 4B) and perpendicular (Figure 4K) to the spindle axis.
evidence: Concluded from the laser ablation experiments showing centrosome motion in both directions

claim: The final length of the spindle is determined by a balance of pulling forces acting in different directions on centrosomes.
source: This observation is consistent with the hypothesis that the final length of the spindle is determined by a balance of pulling forces acting in different directions on centrosomes (Figure 4M).
evidence: Inferred from the laser ablation experiments

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, MTs nucleate from centrosomes at rate γ.
source: In this model, MTs nucleate from centrosomes at rate γ
evidence: Stated as a parameter of the mathematical model

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, MTs grow with velocity Vg.
source: grow with velocity Vg
evidence: Stated as a parameter of the mathematical model

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, MTs undergo catastrophe at rate λ.
source: and undergo catastrophe at rate λ.
evidence: Stated as a parameter of the mathematical model

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, if a MT contacts an unoccupied CFG, it binds and is pulled upon with force f0 along the direction of the MT.
source: If a MT contacts an unoccupied CFG, it binds and is pulled upon with force f0 along the direction of the MT (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated as a feature of the mathematical model

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, only one MT can bind a CFG at a time due to stoichiometric interactions.
source: Due to the stoichiometric nature of the interaction between molecular motors and MTs, only one MT can bind a CFG at a time.
evidence: Stated as a key feature of the mathematical model based on biochemical properties

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, bound MTs detach from CFGs with rate κ.
source: Bound MTs detach from CFGs with rate κ, leaving the CFG unoccupied (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated as a parameter of the mathematical model

claim: Stoichiometric interactions lead to a competition of centrosomes for cortical force generators.
source: Stoichiometric interactions lead to a competition of centrosomes for cortical force generators and yield a stable final position.
evidence: Stated as a key feature and consequence of the Stoichiometric Model

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, centrosomes always move to the same final positions regardless of their starting positions.
source: We repeated this simulation with centrosomes starting from different positions and found that centrosomes always move to the same final positions (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5D

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, a balance of pulling forces stably positions centrosomes.
source: Thus, in the Stoichiometric Model, a balance of pulling forces stably positions centrosomes.
evidence: Concluded from the simulation results

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, centrosomes stably positioned irrespective of the number of CFGs, even with 100,000 CFGs (ten times more than MTs).
source: The centrosomes stably positioned irrespective of the number of CFGs -- even for simulations with 100,000 CFGs, ten times more CFGs than MTs (the largest number of CFGs we investigated, Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by simulation results testing various CFG numbers

claim: A limited number of CFGs does not explain the stable positioning of centrosomes in the Stoichiometric Model.
source: Thus, a limited number of CFGs does not explain the stable positioning of centrosomes in our model.
evidence: Concluded from simulations with varying numbers of CFGs

claim: In simulations without stoichiometric interactions, centrosome positions are always unstable and the centrosomes migrate until they contact the cell periphery.
source: In these simulations, the centrosome's positions are always unstable, and the centrosomes migrate until they contact the cell periphery (Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: The stoichiometric interaction of MTs and CFGs allows cortical pulling forces to stably position centrosomes.
source: Thus, the stoichiometric interaction of MTs and CFGs allows cortical pulling forces to stably position centrosomes.
evidence: Concluded from comparing simulations with and without stoichiometric interactions

claim: Cortical pulling forces with stoichiometric interactions are stabilizing even when the number of CFGs are greater than the number of MTs.
source: Cortical pulling forces with stoichiometric interactions are stabilizing even when the number of CFGs are greater than the number of MTs.
evidence: Concluded from simulation results with varying CFG numbers

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, when a MT from one centrosome binds an CFG, MTs from the other centrosome are prevented from binding to that CFG.
source: This occurs because when a MT from one centrosome binds an CFG, MTs from the other centrosome are prevented from binding to that CFG.
evidence: Stated as a consequence of stoichiometric interactions in the model

claim: In simulations, the probabilities of attachment of CFGs from one centrosome are reduced by the presence of a second centrosome.
source: This effect is evident in our simulations, where the probabilities of attachment of CFGs from one centrosome are reduced by the presence of a second centrosome (Figure 5—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4

claim: In simulations, removing one centrosome allows the remaining centrosome to move to the cell center.
source: A consequence of this competition is that removing one centrosome in the simulation allows the remaining centrosome to interact more strongly with CFGs at the center of the cell, which thus moves the centrosome to the cell center (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: After ablation of one centrosome, the other centrosome moved to the cell center in experiments.
source: After ablation of one centrosome, the other centrosome moved to the cell center (Figure 6D, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Consistent centering of the remaining centrosome after ablation of one centrosome was observed in 13 embryos.
source: We repeated this experiment for 13 embryos and observed a consistent centering of the remaining centrosome (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 13 embryos shown in Figure 6E

claim: The agreement between simulations and experiment argues that the presence of one centrosome modulates the forces acting on the other centrosome.
source: The agreement between simulations and experiment strongly argues that the presence of one centrosome modulates the forces acting on the other centrosome, which is a key prediction of the Stoichiometric Model.
evidence: Concluded from the agreement between simulation predictions and experimental observations

claim: The posterior side of the cortex in C. elegans has approximately 50% more CFGs than the anterior side.
source: Previous studies in C. elegans have shown that the posterior side of the cortex has ~50% more CFGs than the anterior side (Grill et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grill et al., 2003 and Redemann et al., 2010

claim: Simulations with asymmetric CFG distribution accurately reproduce the dynamics of spindle elongation.
source: These simulations with an asymmetric distribution of CFGs accurately reproduce the dynamics of spindle elongation (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Simulations with asymmetric CFG distribution accurately reproduce spindle positioning.
source: and spindle positioning (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: In both experiments and simulations with symmetric CFG distribution (par-6 RNAi), the spindle positioned in the middle of the cell and obtained the same final spindle length as controls.
source: To investigate if the Stoichiometric Model can also account for the behavior of spindle with symmetric distribution of CFGs, we studied spindles in par-6 (RNAi), which greatly expands the size of the PAR-2 domain (Goehring et al., 2011). In both experiments and simulations, the spindle positioned in the middle of the cell and obtained the same final spindle length as controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental and simulation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citation to Goehring et al., 2011

claim: In simulations, spindles in smaller cells have a slower rate of elongation, reach a smaller final length, and position less asymmetrically.
source: In these simulations, spindles in smaller cells have a slower rate of elongation, reach a smaller final length, and position less asymmetrically (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7G and H

claim: The Stoichiometric Model reproduces the scaling of final spindle length with cell length observed across the RIAILs (regression coefficient = 0.52±0.02 for theory vs 0.47±0.02 for RIAILs, p = 0.08).
source: This model reproduces the scaling of final spindle length with cell length observed across the RIAILs (Figure 7I, red, theory, regression coefficient = 0.52±0.02; light blue, RIAILs, regression coefficient = 0.47±0.02, p = 0.08).
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data shown in Figure 7I with statistical analysis (p = 0.08)

claim: The scaling of final spindle length in simulations is in quantitative agreement with its scaling across natural isolates (regression coefficient = 0.46±0.05, p = 0.27).
source: The scaling of final spindle length in the simulations is also in quantitative agreement with its scaling across natural isolates and across different species (Figure 7I, dark blue, natural isolates, regression coefficient = 0.46±0.05, p = 0.27
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data shown in Figure 7I with statistical analysis (p = 0.27)

claim: The scaling of final spindle length in simulations is in quantitative agreement with its scaling across different nematode species (regression coefficient = 0.57±0.10, p = 0.62).
source: purple, nematode species, regression coefficient = 0.57±0.10, p = 0.62).
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data with statistical analysis (p = 0.62)

claim: The Stoichiometric Model reproduces the scaling of centrosome distance from the cortex with cell length across RIAILs, natural isolates, and nematode species.
source: The Stoichiometric Model also reproduces the scaling of centrosome distance from the cortex with cell length, the scaling of the final position of spindle center with cell length, and the scaling of the elongation rate with cell length across RIAILs, natural isolates, and nematode species (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data shown in Figure 7J

claim: The Stoichiometric Model reproduces the scaling of the final position of spindle center with cell length across RIAILs, natural isolates, and nematode species.
source: The Stoichiometric Model also reproduces the scaling of centrosome distance from the cortex with cell length, the scaling of the final position of spindle center with cell length, and the scaling of the elongation rate with cell length across RIAILs, natural isolates, and nematode species (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data shown in Figure 7J

claim: The Stoichiometric Model reproduces the scaling of the elongation rate with cell length across RIAILs, natural isolates, and nematode species.
source: The Stoichiometric Model also reproduces the scaling of centrosome distance from the cortex with cell length, the scaling of the final position of spindle center with cell length, and the scaling of the elongation rate with cell length across RIAILs, natural isolates, and nematode species (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data shown in Figure 7J

claim: The Stoichiometric Model explains the scaling of spindle traits both within and between species.
source: Thus, the Stoichiometric Model explains the scaling of spindle traits both within and between species.
evidence: Concluded from the quantitative agreement between simulations and experimental data across multiple datasets

claim: Spindle elongation and asymmetric positioning in C. elegans are driven by cortical pulling forces acting unevenly on the two centrosomes.
source: Previous studies have shown that spindle elongation and asymmetric positioning in C. elegans are driven by cortical pulling forces acting unevenly on the two centrosomes (Grill et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grill et al., 2003

claim: Laser ablation experiments and genetic perturbations show that spindle elasticity and pushing forces do not significantly contribute to the final position of centrosomes in C. elegans embryos.
source: Our laser ablation experiments and genetic perturbations show that spindle elasticity and pushing forces do not significantly contribute to the final position of centrosomes in C. elegans embryos.
evidence: Concluded from the laser ablation and spd-1 (RNAi) experiments

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, each CFG can only bind one MT at a time.
source: In this model, each CFG can only bind one MT at a time (i.e. the interactions are stoichiometric)
evidence: Stated as a key feature of the Stoichiometric Model

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, every MT that is attached to a CFG experiences the same magnitude of pulling force, irrespective of the MT's length.
source: and every MT that is attached to a CFG, experiences the same magnitude of pulling force, irrespective of the MT's length.
evidence: Stated as a feature of the Stoichiometric Model

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, the stable positioning of centrosomes results from the stoichiometric interaction between MTs and CFGs.
source: In this model, the stable positioning of centrosomes results from the stoichiometric interaction between MTs and CFGs, which prevents the destabilizing feedback present in previous models of cortical pulling forces.
evidence: Stated as a key conclusion about the mechanism of the Stoichiometric Model

claim: Cortical pulling forces are sufficient to stably position centrosomes even in the absence of explicit length dependent forces or a limiting number of CFGs.
source: Thus, cortical pulling forces are sufficient to stably position centrosomes even in the absence of explicit length dependent forces or a limiting number of CFGs.
evidence: Concluded from the analysis of the Stoichiometric Model

claim: The Stoichiometric Model quantitatively explains the asymmetry in positioning of the spindle center by an uneven distribution of CFGs between the anterior and posterior halves of the embryo.
source: The Stoichiometric Model quantitatively explains the asymmetry in positioning of the spindle center by an uneven distribution of CFGs between the anterior and posterior halves of the embryo.
evidence: Concluded from simulations with asymmetric CFG distribution

claim: The Stoichiometric Model accounts for variations in all the spindle traits studied across nematode species spanning over 100 million years of evolution.
